# Illinois Condo Repairs: Owner Responsibility vs. Association

CenterPoint Association Management Published August 13, 2026 3 min read

A pipe leaks, a window fails, a balcony railing rusts, and the first question is never how do we fix it but whose bill is this? More friction between owners and associations begins here than anywhere else, and most of it is avoidable, because the answer follows a structure that every Illinois condominium shares.

## Who is responsible for condo repairs in Illinois?
As a general rule, the unit owner maintains everything inside the unit, interior surfaces, fixtures, appliances, and improvements, while the association maintains the common elements: the structure, roof, facade, common piping, hallways, and building systems. A third category, limited common elements such as balconies and windows, serves a single unit but sits on the building, and responsibility for those goes whichever way the association's declaration assigns it.

## The Three Zones, Defined
The Illinois Condominium Property Act (765 ILCS 605) gives every condominium the same legal anatomy. The **unit** is the space you own outright, typically from the interior finished surfaces inward. The **common elements** are everything else: land, structure, roof, mechanical systems, corridors, and amenities, owned by all unit owners together as percentages. **Limited common elements** are the hybrid zone, portions of the common elements reserved for one unit's exclusive use, most famously balconies, terraces, parking spaces, and, in many declarations, windows and entry doors.

## What the Owner Almost Always Maintains

- **Interior surfaces:** drywall, paint, wallpaper, and flooring.
- **Fixtures and appliances:** faucets, toilets, garbage disposals, dishwashers, in-unit laundry.
- **In-unit systems:** electrical outlets and fixtures from the panel in, plumbing from the branch shutoff in, and HVAC equipment that serves only that unit.
- **Improvements:** anything a current or previous owner installed, built-ins, upgraded counters, that rainfall shower, including the day it leaks.

## What the Association Almost Always Maintains

- **Structure and envelope:** foundation, framing, roof, facade, masonry, and tuckpointing.
- **Common systems:** risers and stacks, common electrical, central boilers, elevators, and life-safety equipment.
- **Shared spaces:** lobbies, corridors, stairwells, amenity rooms, grounds, and parking structures.

## Who pays for balcony and window repairs in a condo?
It depends entirely on the declaration. Balconies and windows are usually limited common elements, and Illinois declarations split three ways: some assign the full cost to the association, some to the owner who has exclusive use, and many split it, the owner handles cleaning and minor upkeep while the association handles structural repair and replacement. Boards may also charge limited-common-element costs back to the benefited unit where the declaration authorizes it. Read the maintenance article of your declaration before assuming either way.

## When Water Crosses the Line
Water damage is where the zones collide. The working principle: responsibility follows the source, and insurance follows the declaration. If a common riser bursts and ruins your ceiling, the association repairs the riser and typically the building-standard portions of your unit its policy covers, while your own [HO-6 policy](https://www.centerpointmgmt.com/condo-living#insurance) picks up your upgrades, your belongings, and any master-policy deductible your declaration passes through to affected units. If your supply line fails and floods the unit below, expect both policies, and both deductibles, to enter the conversation.

## The Five-Minute Habit That Prevents the Fight
Before hiring a contractor or demanding a repair from the board, spend five minutes with two documents: the **maintenance matrix** in your declaration (usually an article titled "Maintenance, Repair and Replacement") and the association's **insurance boundary**. In CenterPoint-managed buildings both live in the resident portal's document library, and our team answers responsibility questions before work begins, because a repair assigned correctly on day one never becomes a dispute on day thirty.
